sub: Web architecture, client-server communication, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS and hosting
q: A browser re-requests a cached stylesheet, sending If-None-Match with the ETag it stored. The file on the server has not changed. Which status code should the server return?

opts.A: 200 OK, with the stylesheet body
opts.B: 204 No Content
opts.C: 304 Not Modified
opts.D: 412 Precondition Failed

exp: A conditional GET whose validator still matches is answered with 304 Not Modified and no message body, telling the browser its cached copy is still usable. 204 also carries no body but means the request succeeded with nothing to return, not that a cached representation is fresh, and 412 reports a precondition that failed on an unsafe request.

sub: Web architecture, client-server communication, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS and hosting
q: A day before migrating a web application to a new server, the administrator drops the TTL on the site's DNS A record from 86400 to 300 seconds. What does this achieve?

opts.A: Resolver caches expire quickly, so clients pick up the new IP address soon after the record is changed
opts.B: The registrar propagates the change to all root name servers immediately
opts.C: The authoritative name server gains extra query capacity for the duration of the migration
opts.D: The old server begins refusing new connections as soon as the record is changed

exp: TTL tells recursive resolvers how long they may keep serving a cached answer, so shrinking it ahead of a planned change limits how long a stale IP address stays in circulation. Root name servers hold no A record for the site, and DNS has no way to tell resolvers to discard an answer early, which is exactly why the TTL has to be lowered in advance rather than at cutover.

sub: Web architecture, client-server communication, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS and hosting
q: Dozens of HTTPS sites share a single IP address on a hosting server. Which mechanism lets the server pick the right TLS certificate for the site the client asked for?

opts.A: The HTTP Host header carried in the request
opts.B: The Server Name Indication extension in the TLS ClientHello
opts.C: ALPN negotiation of the application protocol
opts.D: OCSP stapling of the certificate's revocation status

exp: SNI puts the requested hostname in the ClientHello, before any certificate has been chosen, which is precisely what name-based HTTPS virtual hosting needs. The Host header cannot serve this purpose because it travels inside the encrypted request, which only exists after the handshake has already committed to a certificate.

sub: HTML, semantic elements, forms, multimedia, Canvas, SVG and accessibility
q: A dashboard must plot a scatter chart of 50,000 points and redraw it on every mouse drag. Why is a canvas element normally preferred here over inline SVG?

opts.A: SVG cannot be scripted from JavaScript once the document has loaded
opts.B: Only canvas supports colour gradients and opacity
opts.C: Canvas draws pixels immediately and keeps no node per point, avoiding the layout and hit-testing cost of a 50,000-element tree
opts.D: Canvas drawings are exposed to assistive technology automatically, so no fallback is needed

exp: Canvas is an immediate-mode raster surface: the drawing calls leave behind no retained objects, so the cost is the draw itself and nothing more. SVG keeps every point as a DOM element the browser must style, lay out and hit-test, which is what makes very large, continuously redrawn datasets slow; canvas is in fact the weaker of the two for accessibility, needing explicit fallback content.

sub: HTML, semantic elements, forms, multimedia, Canvas, SVG and accessibility
q: A text input is given only a placeholder attribute and no associated label element. What is the accessibility defect?

opts.A: Placeholder text cannot be restyled with CSS
opts.B: Screen readers announce the placeholder twice
opts.C: The input is omitted from the form submission
opts.D: The placeholder disappears once the user types, and it is not a reliable accessible name for the field

exp: A placeholder is a hint, not a name: it vanishes as soon as the field has a value, leaving the user with no persistent statement of what the field is, and its exposure as an accessible name is inconsistent across assistive technology. A label bound to the input's id gives a permanent, reliably announced name and enlarges the clickable target as a bonus.

sub: HTML, semantic elements, forms, multimedia, Canvas, SVG and accessibility
q: Inside a form element, a developer writes a button element with no type attribute, and the user clicks it. What happens by default?

opts.A: The form is submitted
opts.B: The form's fields are reset to their initial values
opts.C: Nothing happens until a click handler is attached
opts.D: The button behaves as type="button" and only runs its own handler

exp: The missing-value default for a button's type is submit, so the click submits the owning form and the page navigates away, which is a common reason a handler appears to run and then lose its work. Writing type="button" explicitly is what makes the element inert with respect to submission.

sub: CSS, Flexbox, Grid and responsive web design
q: Four items sit in a flex row and one holds far more text than the others. Which declaration on the items makes all four end up the same width, assuming no item contains an unbreakable token wider than its share?

opts.A: flex: 1 1 auto
opts.B: flex: 1 1 0
opts.C: flex-shrink: 0
opts.D: justify-content: space-between on the container

exp: Equal widths require growth to start from a zero base: a flex-basis of 0 discards each item's content-derived size, so the container's free space is the only thing being divided and equal flex-grow divides it evenly. With a basis of auto the content width is the starting point, so the text-heavy item stays wider even though every item grows at the same rate. Flex items do default to min-width: auto, so an item is never laid out narrower than its min-content size -- equalising truly regardless of content also needs min-width: 0.

sub: CSS, Flexbox, Grid and responsive web design
q: A card container is styled grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr)). What layout does this produce as the container is made narrower?

opts.A: A fixed column count whose cards shrink below 220px
opts.B: A single 220px column at every viewport width
opts.C: As many columns of at least 220px as fit, dropping to fewer columns as space runs out, with the columns sharing any leftover space equally
opts.D: One column per card, scrolling horizontally once they no longer fit

exp: auto-fill asks the grid for as many tracks as the container can hold, while minmax(220px, 1fr) sets each track's floor at 220px and lets it absorb an equal share of the surplus. The track count therefore falls as the container narrows, which is how a responsive card grid is built without writing a media query at all.

sub: CSS, Flexbox, Grid and responsive web design
q: A site's media queries are written correctly, yet on a phone the full desktop layout appears shrunk to fit the screen. What is missing?

opts.A: A viewport meta tag declaring width=device-width, initial-scale=1
opts.B: A max-width: 100% rule on the body element
opts.C: The screen keyword on each media query
opts.D: A second stylesheet linked with a media attribute

exp: Without that meta tag a mobile browser assumes a layout viewport of roughly 980px and then scales the rendered page down to the device, so min-width breakpoints are evaluated against the fictitious wide viewport and the mobile rules never match. Setting the layout viewport to the device width lets the media queries see the real dimensions.

sub: JavaScript, the DOM, event handling, asynchronous programming, JSON and Fetch

opts.A: A, B, C, D
opts.B: A, D, C, B
opts.C: A, D, B, C
opts.D: A, C, D, B

exp: The synchronous statements run to completion first, logging A then D. When the call stack empties the microtask queue is drained before any macrotask, so the already-resolved promise's callback logs C. The setTimeout callback is a timer task and only runs after that, logging B: a zero-millisecond delay does not promote it ahead of a microtask.

sub: JavaScript, the DOM, event handling, asynchronous programming, JSON and Fetch
q: A fetch call to an endpoint that responds 500 Internal Server Error with a JSON error body is made. What does the returned promise do?

opts.A: Rejects with an error describing the 500 response
opts.B: Resolves with null, since the body is not a successful payload
opts.C: Rejects, because only 2xx responses resolve
opts.D: Resolves with a Response whose ok is false and whose status is 500

exp: fetch rejects only when the request itself fails, such as a DNS failure, a refused connection, a CORS refusal or an abort, and treats any completed HTTP exchange as a success however unhappy the status line. Code must therefore test response.ok or response.status before reading the body, which is why omitting that check lets server errors flow silently down the success path.

sub: JavaScript, the DOM, event handling, asynchronous programming, JSON and Fetch
q: A table body is filled with rows created after page load, and one click listener is attached to the tbody element. Inside the handler, which property refers to the element the user actually clicked?

opts.A: event.currentTarget
opts.B: this, in a normal function listener
opts.C: event.target
opts.D: event.srcTarget

exp: As an event bubbles, target stays fixed on the deepest element where it originated, whereas currentTarget, and this in a normal function listener, refer to the tbody the listener is bound to. That distinction is the whole basis of event delegation: one listener on a stable ancestor, with target and closest() identifying which dynamically added descendant was hit.

sub: Frontend frameworks: components, routing, state management and API integration
q: A single-page app uses history-based client-side routing. In-app navigation to /reports/7 works, but reloading the browser on that URL returns 404 from the web server. What is required?

opts.A: Switch the router to hash-based URLs, since history-based routing cannot be served over HTTP
opts.B: Register /reports/:id as a server-side route that renders the report itself
opts.C: Configure the web server to fall back to index.html for unmatched paths so the client router can resolve the URL
opts.D: Add a router redirect from /reports/7 back to /

exp: Client-side routing only exists once the app's JavaScript is running, so a cold request for a deep path is an ordinary HTTP request for a file the server does not have. A catch-all rewrite to index.html, such as try_files with an index.html fallback in Nginx, lets the bundle load and then resolve the path itself; redirecting to the root would stop the 404 but throw away the URL the user asked for.

sub: Frontend frameworks: components, routing, state management and API integration
q: In a framework's controlled form input, where does the value shown in the field come from on every render?

opts.A: The DOM node's own internal value, which the component reads back when the form is submitted
opts.B: Component state, with a change handler writing each keystroke back into that state
opts.C: The defaultValue attribute, mutated in place by the browser
opts.D: A two-way binding maintained by the browser's autofill machinery

exp: A controlled input's value is driven from state, so state is the single source of truth and the DOM node merely reflects it; the change handler exists precisely to put the user's keystroke into state so the next render shows it. The other arrangement is the uncontrolled input, where the DOM holds the value and the component reads it out through a ref when it needs it.

sub: Frontend frameworks: components, routing, state management and API integration
q: A search component fetches results whenever the query changes. A slow response for an earlier query can arrive after a faster response for a later one, briefly showing results for the wrong query. What is the standard fix?

opts.A: Debounce the input so requests are issued less often
opts.B: Move the fetch into the render body so it re-runs synchronously
opts.C: Send the requests with POST instead of GET
opts.D: Cancel or ignore the superseded request in the effect's cleanup, so only the latest query's response is applied

exp: This is a race, not a rate problem, so correctness has to come from discarding stale responses: the effect's cleanup either aborts the in-flight request through an AbortController or sets a flag the resolved handler checks before touching state. Debouncing only makes the race less frequent, and fetching during render breaks render purity and can loop.

sub: Backend development in PHP and Python: REST APIs, CRUD, middleware, auth, sessions and ORM
q: A client's request times out and it retries. Which HTTP method's semantics guarantee that the retry cannot create a second copy of the resource?

opts.A: POST
opts.B: PUT
opts.C: PATCH
opts.D: POST accompanied by a Retry-After response header

exp: PUT is idempotent: it means make the resource at this URI equal to this representation, so applying it twice leaves the same end state as applying it once and a blind retry is safe. POST creates a new subordinate resource at a server-chosen URI and stays non-idempotent whatever headers accompany it, and PATCH is not idempotent in general because a delta such as increment by one compounds on replay.

sub: Backend development in PHP and Python: REST APIs, CRUD, middleware, auth, sessions and ORM
q: With PHP's default session handling, what does the cookie sent to the browser contain?

opts.A: The serialised contents of the $_SESSION array
opts.B: A signed copy of the session data, which the server verifies on each request
opts.C: The user's credentials, encrypted with the session key
opts.D: Only a session identifier, with the session data held server-side

exp: Calling session_start() issues an opaque identifier, PHPSESSID by default, and keeps the data itself in a server-side session store, so the cookie is nothing more than a pointer into that store. A signed cookie carrying the session payload is a different design that some frameworks use: stateless and horizontally scalable, but with the data genuinely in the client's hands and a correspondingly different threat model.

sub: Backend development in PHP and Python: REST APIs, CRUD, middleware, auth, sessions and ORM
q: A Python view iterates 100 order records and reads order.customer.name on each, and the ORM issues 101 queries. What is this, and how is it removed?

opts.A: A lazy-loading N+1 problem, removed by eager-loading the related rows in the initial query
opts.B: Connection-pool exhaustion, removed by raising the pool size
opts.C: A transaction isolation problem, removed by moving to serialisable isolation
opts.D: A cache miss storm, removed by holding each customer row in a memory cache

exp: One query fetches the orders and each lazy attribute access fires another for its customer, which is the classic N+1 whose cost grows linearly with the row count. Eager loading, through select_related or prefetch_related in Django and joinedload or selectinload in SQLAlchemy, collapses it to a small constant number of queries; caching only hides the pattern and still pays it on every cold key.

sub: Git version control, Docker, CI/CD, Linux administration, Nginx and deployment
q: A defective commit has already been pushed to a shared main branch. Which command undoes its effect without rewriting published history?

opts.A: git reset --hard HEAD~1
opts.B: git revert on that commit
opts.C: git rebase -i HEAD~2, dropping the commit
opts.D: git checkout HEAD~1 -- .

exp: git revert records a new commit whose diff is the inverse of the offending one, so the branch stays append-only and every collaborator's clone fast-forwards cleanly. A hard reset and an interactive rebase both rewrite existing commits, which on a shared branch means a force push and broken working copies for anyone who has already pulled.

sub: Git version control, Docker, CI/CD, Linux administration, Nginx and deployment
q: Nginx serves a static site from /var/www/site/. For the worker process's user to read /var/www/site/index.html, which permission must it hold on /var, /var/www and /var/www/site?

opts.A: Write permission
opts.B: Read permission only
opts.C: Execute, that is search, permission
opts.D: Ownership of each directory

exp: On a directory the execute bit means may traverse, and resolving a path requires traversing every component of it, so a missing x anywhere up the chain produces a 403 even when the file itself is world-readable. Read permission on a directory only permits listing the names it contains, which is not what path resolution needs.

sub: Git version control, Docker, CI/CD, Linux administration, Nginx and deployment
q: A CI pipeline builds a Docker image for a web application. Why should the application's secret API key be supplied as a run-time environment variable rather than written into the Dockerfile with ENV?

opts.A: ENV variables set in a Dockerfile are not visible to the application process at run time
opts.B: Run-time variables are encrypted by the container runtime whereas build-time ones are not
opts.C: ENV values are length-limited and would truncate the key
opts.D: Anything set in the Dockerfile is baked into an inspectable image layer, so anyone who can pull the image can read the secret

exp: Image layers and their build metadata are readable with docker history and docker inspect by anyone who obtains the image, so a secret committed at build time is published along with it and survives in the registry and in every derived image. Injecting it at run time from the orchestrator's secret store keeps the artefact itself free of credentials; the runtime does not encrypt environment variables either way.

sub: Web security: OWASP Top 10, SSL/TLS, CSRF, XSS and SQL injection prevention
q: Which measure reliably prevents SQL injection in a PHP application querying MySQL?

opts.A: Prepared statements with bound parameters, so user input never becomes part of the SQL text
opts.B: Passing every input through addslashes() before concatenating it into the query
opts.C: Stripping quote and semicolon characters from all input with str_replace()
opts.D: Disabling error display so the database's messages never reach the attacker

exp: Binding sends the statement and the data along separate paths, so the database treats input as a value that can never be reparsed as syntax, which makes the injection structurally impossible rather than merely filtered. Escaping and character blacklisting are both bypassable, notably in numeric contexts where no quote is needed at all, and hiding errors removes only the attacker's feedback while the hole stays open.

sub: Web security: OWASP Top 10, SSL/TLS, CSRF, XSS and SQL injection prevention
q: An application authenticates users with a session cookie and takes no further precaution. What makes a CSRF attack against it possible?

opts.A: JavaScript on the attacker's page can read the session cookie's value
opts.B: The browser attaches the cookie automatically to requests that the attacker's page triggers towards the application
opts.C: The attacker can read the application's responses from a cross-origin page
opts.D: The session identifier is predictable enough to be guessed

exp: CSRF exploits ambient authority: the browser sends the victim's cookie with any request to that origin, including a form post or image load initiated by an unrelated site, so the server sees a fully authenticated request the user never intended. The attacker needs neither to read the cookie nor to see the response, which is why an unguessable identifier does not help and why the defences are an unpredictable per-request token plus SameSite cookies.

sub: Web security: OWASP Top 10, SSL/TLS, CSRF, XSS and SQL injection prevention
q: User-supplied comment text is inserted into a page with element.innerHTML = comment. Which change reliably removes the cross-site scripting risk at this sink, independently of how the value was stored?

opts.A: Assign to element.textContent instead, so the string becomes a text node and is never parsed as markup
opts.B: HTML-escape the comment once when it is stored in the database and keep using innerHTML
opts.C: Remove script tags from the comment with a regular expression before assigning it
opts.D: Wrap the comment in encodeURIComponent() before assigning it

exp: textContent creates a text node, so angle brackets and attributes stay inert characters and there is no HTML parse step left to hijack, whatever is already in the database. Tag blacklisting fails against event-handler payloads such as an img element with an onerror attribute, and encodeURIComponent is a URL encoding and wrong for an HTML context. Escaping once at storage time does neutralise this sink, but it leaves every row stored before the change untouched, corrupts the value for every non-HTML consumer, and protects no sink added later.

sub: Architecture and scale: MVC, microservices, SOLID, event-driven systems, caching and queues
q: A payment class contains a switch over payment types, and adding a new payment type always means editing that switch. Which SOLID principle does this violate?

opts.A: Single Responsibility Principle
opts.B: Interface Segregation Principle
opts.C: Liskov Substitution Principle
opts.D: Open/Closed Principle

exp: Open/Closed asks that behaviour be extensible without modifying existing, already-tested code, and a central switch forces exactly that modification for every new case. Replacing it with a common payment interface and one implementation per type lets a new type arrive as new code only. Single Responsibility concerns how many reasons a class has to change, not whether extending it requires an edit.

sub: Architecture and scale: MVC, microservices, SOLID, event-driven systems, caching and queues
q: In the MVC pattern as applied to web frameworks, what is the controller's primary responsibility?

opts.A: Holding the application's business rules and persistence logic
opts.B: Generating the HTML or JSON that is sent to the client
opts.C: Interpreting the incoming request, invoking the appropriate model operations and selecting what to render in response
opts.D: Owning the database connection pool and transaction boundaries for the whole application

exp: The controller is the request-handling seam: it translates parameters, delegates the real work to the model and decides which view or representation answers the request. Business rules and persistence belong to the model and markup to the view, and collapsing either into the controller produces the fat controller that makes MVC code hard to test in isolation.

sub: Architecture and scale: MVC, microservices, SOLID, event-driven systems, caching and queues
q: A heavily read cache key expires and thousands of concurrent requests all miss and hit the database at once, overloading it. What is this failure mode, and what is a standard mitigation?

opts.A: A cache stampede, mitigated by letting one request rebuild the entry under a lock while the others serve the stale value, and by jittering expiry times
opts.B: A write-through inconsistency, mitigated by moving to a write-back cache
opts.C: Cache poisoning, mitigated by signing each cache entry
opts.D: Eviction thrash, mitigated by changing the policy from LRU to LFU

exp: When a hot entry expires every concurrent reader misses simultaneously, so the cache stops absorbing load at exactly the moment it is needed most; this is the stampede, or thundering herd. Serialising the rebuild so only one request recomputes the value, and spreading TTLs with random jitter so keys do not expire in lockstep, are the usual answers, whereas an eviction policy change addresses capacity pressure, which is a different problem.

sub: AI-assisted web development, generative AI APIs, Model Context Protocol, analytics, ethics and law
q: In the Model Context Protocol (MCP), what is the role of an MCP server in relation to the LLM application that connects to it?

opts.A: It holds the language model weights and runs inference on behalf of the client
opts.B: It exposes tools, resources and prompts that the client application can discover and invoke
opts.C: It fine-tunes the model on the organisation's private documents before each session
opts.D: It caches the client's earlier completions so repeated prompts cost fewer tokens

exp: MCP is an open protocol that separates the host application and its client from servers which publish capabilities over a standard transport: tools the model can call, resources it can read, and reusable prompt templates. Inference stays with the model provider, so adding a new data source means writing or configuring a server rather than hand-coding another bespoke integration.

sub: AI-assisted web development, generative AI APIs, Model Context Protocol, analytics, ethics and law
q: A single-page frontend calls a hosted generative AI API directly from browser JavaScript, sending the provider's API key from a build-time environment variable. Why must this be moved behind a backend proxy before going to production?

opts.A: The browser cannot set an Authorization header on a cross-origin request
opts.B: The provider requires the model name to be selected server-side, not by the client
opts.C: A streamed response body cannot be read incrementally by browser JavaScript
opts.D: The key is inlined into the shipped bundle at build time and is readable by any visitor

exp: Build tools substitute environment variables into the client bundle as literal text, so a key placed there ships to every visitor and can be extracted from the JavaScript or the network tab and used to bill the account. A server-side proxy keeps the credential private and is also the only place you can enforce your own per-user authentication, quotas and prompt-injection filtering. Cross-origin requests may carry an Authorization header whenever CORS permits it, so option A is not the obstacle.

sub: AI-assisted web development, generative AI APIs, Model Context Protocol, analytics, ethics and law
q: A state government portal wants to embed a third-party web analytics script that sets a persistent cookie to identify returning visitors and report on their journeys. Under the consent framework of the DPDP Act 2023, what does the portal have to get right first?

opts.A: Give a clear notice of purpose and obtain free, specific, informed consent before the tracking identifier is set, with a means to withdraw it
opts.B: Keep the collected analytics data on servers located outside India so the Act's obligations do not attach
opts.C: Anonymise the stored data after a fixed retention period, which cures the absence of consent retrospectively
opts.D: Designate the analytics vendor as the data fiduciary so that responsibility passes from the portal to the vendor

exp: The DPDP Act is built on notice and consent: consent must be free, specific, informed and capable of being withdrawn, and it must follow a notice stating the purpose, so a tracking cookie should not be written on first paint. Because the portal decides the purpose and means of processing it remains the data fiduciary, and the analytics vendor processing on its behalf is a data processor, so contractual labelling does not transfer the duty; nor does storing the data abroad, since the Act reaches processing of personal data of individuals in India.

sub: Distributed, edge and cloud computing; NIST cloud architecture
q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five essential characteristics of cloud computing in the NIST definition?

opts.A: Rapid elasticity
opts.B: Resource pooling
opts.C: Provider-managed disaster recovery
opts.D: Measured service

exp: NIST lists exactly five essential characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service. Disaster recovery is commonly sold as a managed offering, but it is a product a provider may choose to sell rather than a defining property of cloud computing, so it is the odd one out.

sub: Distributed, edge and cloud computing; NIST cloud architecture
q: In the NIST cloud computing reference architecture, which actor is responsible for providing the connectivity and transport of cloud services between provider and consumer?

opts.A: Cloud broker
opts.B: Cloud carrier
opts.C: Cloud auditor
opts.D: Cloud provider

exp: The reference architecture names five actors — consumer, provider, carrier, broker and auditor — and assigns the network and telecommunication transport role to the cloud carrier. A cloud broker is the tempting distractor: it negotiates, aggregates and intermediates services on the consumer's behalf, but it does not carry the traffic.

sub: Distributed, edge and cloud computing; NIST cloud architecture
q: An assembly-line inspection system must accept or reject each part within 20 ms of capturing its image. The nearest cloud region has a measured round-trip time of 60 ms. Running the inference model on an edge node inside the plant primarily removes which constraint?

opts.A: The wide-area round-trip time, which on its own already exceeds the control loop's deadline
opts.B: The need to encrypt the inspection images while they are in transit
opts.C: A shortage of accelerator capacity in cloud regions
opts.D: An inability of cloud platforms to scale horizontally under load

exp: At 60 ms round trip the network alone consumes three times the entire 20 ms budget before any inference time is counted, so no amount of remote compute can meet the deadline — placing the computation next to the sensor is the only way to fit it. Encryption cost and capacity planning are real concerns, but neither is what makes the deadline unachievable here.

sub: Deployment and service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
q: Which of the following is one of the four cloud deployment models defined by NIST?

opts.A: Virtual private cloud
opts.B: Multi-cloud
opts.C: Distributed cloud
opts.D: Community cloud

exp: NIST defines exactly four deployment models — private, community, public and hybrid — where a community cloud is provisioned for exclusive use by several organisations that share concerns such as mission, policy or compliance regime. Virtual private cloud, multi-cloud and distributed cloud are vendor and industry terms that sit outside that definition.

sub: Deployment and service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
q: A team must run a long-lived Java web application. It wants to deploy its own build artefact and control how many application instances run, but does not want to patch the operating system, the JVM or the web server. Which service model fits this best?

opts.A: IaaS
opts.B: PaaS
opts.C: SaaS
opts.D: Function as a Service

exp: PaaS hands the customer the deployment unit and the instance-count and scaling controls while the provider owns operating system, runtime and middleware patching, which is precisely the split described. FaaS would also hide the OS but is event-driven with short-lived invocations and no long-running instance count to manage, and IaaS would leave OS and JVM patching with the team.

sub: Deployment and service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
q: A serverless function backing a low-traffic internal API responds in about 40 ms most of the time, but the first request after several idle hours takes over two seconds. What is the most likely cause?

opts.A: The platform scaled the function to zero, so a new execution environment has to be initialised before the handler runs
opts.B: DNS records for the API endpoint expiring from cache
opts.C: The function exceeding its configured memory limit
opts.D: The API gateway rate-limiting the first request after an idle period

exp: Scaling to zero when idle is normal for a Function-as-a-Service platform, so with no warm environment available the platform must allocate a sandbox, load the deployment package and initialise the runtime before invoking the handler — the cold start seen only on the first request after idleness. A memory-limit breach would fail the invocation rather than merely delay it, and rate limiting rejects requests rather than slowing them.

sub: Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
q: In a microservices deployment running a service mesh, which task belongs to the sidecar proxies of the data plane rather than to the mesh's control plane?

opts.A: Distributing routing policy and issued workload certificates to the proxies
opts.B: Terminating and originating mutual TLS on each individual service-to-service request and applying its retry and timeout rules
opts.C: Holding the mesh's desired configuration and reconciling drift from it
opts.D: Exposing the operator-facing API through which traffic-shifting rules are declared

exp: The data plane is the set of sidecar proxies that sit directly in the request path — every call into and out of a workload passes through one, which is where mutual TLS, retries, timeouts and per-request telemetry are actually enforced. The control plane never touches an individual request: it computes configuration and issues certificates, then pushes both to those proxies.

sub: Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
q: Which capability requires a Layer 7 load balancer and cannot be provided by a Layer 4 load balancer?

opts.A: Distributing inbound TCP connections across a pool of backends
opts.B: Removing an unhealthy backend from rotation when a health check fails
opts.C: Preserving the client's source IP address towards the backend
opts.D: Sending requests for /api to one backend pool and requests for /static to another

exp: Path-based and Host-header-based routing requires the balancer to parse the HTTP request itself, which only a Layer 7 proxy does; a Layer 4 balancer forwards TCP or UDP flows and never sees the URL. Connection distribution and health checking exist at both layers, and preserving the client source IP is in fact easier at Layer 4 because no proxy hop is introduced.

sub: Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
q: A stateless API autoscales on average CPU evaluated over a five-minute window, but its real traffic arrives as 30-second bursts about ten times an hour. What behaviour is most likely to be observed?

opts.A: The group scales down but never scales back up again
opts.B: The group adds instances continuously until it reaches its maximum size
opts.C: Latency and errors spike during each burst, and whatever instances are added arrive after the burst has already passed
opts.D: The load balancer stops health-checking the group for the duration of each burst

exp: A five-minute averaging window smooths a 30-second burst almost out of existence, and even when it does trigger, provisioning and warm-up complete after the burst is over, so the capacity arrives when it is no longer needed. Elasticity only helps when the control loop reacts faster than the demand it tracks; the fixes here are a shorter evaluation window, a queue to absorb bursts, or holding headroom in reserve.

sub: Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization
q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a Type-1 hypervisor from a Type-2 hypervisor?

opts.A: A Type-1 hypervisor runs directly on the host hardware, while a Type-2 hypervisor runs as a process on top of a host operating system
opts.B: A Type-1 hypervisor requires paravirtualized guests, while a Type-2 hypervisor can run unmodified guests
opts.C: A Type-1 hypervisor can host only Linux guests, while a Type-2 hypervisor can host any operating system
opts.D: A Type-1 hypervisor emulates every device in software, while a Type-2 hypervisor passes all devices straight through to the guest

exp: The classification turns purely on what the hypervisor sits on: a bare-metal Type-1 hypervisor is itself the layer that owns the hardware, whereas a hosted Type-2 hypervisor is an application scheduled by an underlying host operating system. Whether guests need modification is the separate full-versus-paravirtualization question and does not follow from the type.

sub: Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization
q: Under paravirtualization, how does the guest operating system differ from a fully virtualized guest?

opts.A: It runs entirely in ring 0 with no hypervisor mediation of any kind
opts.B: It is presented with emulated hardware indistinguishable from a physical machine and needs no changes
opts.C: It shares the host kernel instead of running a kernel of its own
opts.D: It is modified so that sensitive privileged operations are replaced by explicit hypercalls into the hypervisor

exp: Paravirtualization trades guest portability for speed: the guest kernel is ported to be aware that it is virtualized and calls the hypervisor directly, avoiding the cost of trapping and emulating every privileged instruction. Option B describes full virtualization, where an unmodified guest is deliberately kept unaware, and sharing the host kernel describes containers rather than a virtual machine of either kind.

sub: Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization
q: A provider must let tens of thousands of tenants use overlapping private IPv4 ranges on top of one shared physical fabric. Which network-virtualization approach makes that workable?

opts.A: Assigning each tenant its own physical top-of-rack switch
opts.B: An overlay that encapsulates tenant Layer-2 frames for transport across the fabric, tagging each with a per-tenant network identifier in the encapsulation header
opts.C: 802.1Q VLAN tagging alone, with one VLAN per tenant
opts.D: Source NAT applied at the first-hop router for every tenant

exp: Overlay encapsulation such as VXLAN wraps each tenant's frames in an outer packet carrying a per-tenant segment identifier, so identical addresses in different tenants never meet and the physical fabric only has to route the outer header. A plain 802.1Q VLAN ID is 12 bits, capping usable segments at 4094, which cannot reach tens of thousands of tenants, and per-tenant hardware defeats the purpose of a shared fabric.

sub: Containers, Docker, Kubernetes orchestration, Infrastructure as Code and DevOps
q: A container in a Kubernetes Pod declares a memory request of 256Mi and a memory limit of 512Mi. Which statement about how those two values are used is correct?

opts.A: The scheduler reserves 512Mi on the node and the container is CPU-throttled once it exceeds 256Mi
opts.B: Both values are advisory only and neither is enforced at runtime
opts.C: The container is throttled rather than terminated when its memory usage passes 512Mi
opts.D: The scheduler places the Pod against the 256Mi request, and the container is terminated if its usage exceeds 512Mi

exp: Requests drive scheduling — the scheduler only needs a node with 256Mi of allocatable memory remaining — while limits are enforced at runtime on the node. Memory is an incompressible resource, so a container exceeding its memory limit is killed for being out of memory; throttling is what happens to a container over its CPU limit, which is exactly what makes option C the tempting wrong answer.

sub: Containers, Docker, Kubernetes orchestration, Infrastructure as Code and DevOps
q: Terraform and Ansible are both used to manage infrastructure as code. Which description of the usual division of labour between them is accurate?

opts.A: Both are agent-based and require an agent to be installed on every managed node before use
opts.B: Terraform configures software inside existing servers, while Ansible creates the servers themselves
opts.C: Terraform declares desired infrastructure and reconciles it against recorded state to create, change or destroy resources, while Ansible is primarily agentless configuration management that runs tasks over SSH
opts.D: Terraform is imperative and executes ordered steps, while Ansible is declarative and keeps a state file of what it built

exp: Terraform's model is declarative provisioning plus a state file mapping configuration to real resource identifiers, which is how it knows what to add, change or delete on the next apply; Ansible pushes tasks to hosts over SSH with no agent installed and keeps no comparable state of record. Option D inverts both properties and option B swaps the two tools' primary roles.

sub: Containers, Docker, Kubernetes orchestration, Infrastructure as Code and DevOps
q: Linux containers rest on two distinct kernel mechanisms. Which one caps how much CPU time and memory a container may consume, as opposed to controlling what it can see?

opts.A: Control groups (cgroups)
opts.B: Namespaces
opts.C: Union filesystem layers
opts.D: Seccomp filters

exp: cgroups account for and limit a process group's consumption of resources such as CPU, memory and block I/O, and are the mechanism a container runtime uses to honour a declared resource limit. Namespaces do the other half of the job by isolating the view of PIDs, mounts, network and users; seccomp restricts which system calls may be made, and union layers supply the image filesystem.

sub: Cloud storage, compute, networking, managed databases, monitoring and multi-cloud
q: Which workload is the poorest fit for object storage and should sit on block storage instead?

opts.A: Long-term retention copies of nightly backups
opts.B: Static images and JavaScript files served to browsers
opts.C: A media archive read sequentially by a transcoding job
opts.D: The data files of a transactional relational database doing small random in-place updates

exp: Object storage exposes whole objects over an HTTP API with no partial in-place write and comparatively high per-operation latency, which is the opposite of what a database's small random block updates need; that workload belongs on a block volume the guest can format and write at block granularity. The other three are write-once, read-many patterns that object storage is designed to serve cheaply.

sub: Cloud storage, compute, networking, managed databases, monitoring and multi-cloud
q: A user request passes through eight microservices and is intermittently slow, yet every individual service's own latency dashboard looks normal. Which telemetry most directly identifies which hop is consuming the time?

opts.A: Distributed tracing, with a trace context propagated across every hop so each span's duration is recorded within one request
opts.B: Raising the log level to DEBUG on all eight services
opts.C: Host-level CPU and memory metrics collected at a finer interval
opts.D: An aggregated error-rate counter for each service

exp: Per-service aggregates hide a tail that only some requests hit, whereas a trace follows one request end to end and attributes elapsed time to each span, making the slow hop visible directly. Finer host metrics and error counters describe resource consumption and failures rather than where a single request spent its time, and DEBUG logging across eight services produces volume without a correlating request identifier.

sub: Cloud storage, compute, networking, managed databases, monitoring and multi-cloud
q: An organisation runs the same containerised application on two cloud providers to avoid lock-in. In practice, what most commonly limits that portability?

opts.A: Container image formats being mutually incompatible between providers
opts.B: Differences in the Linux kernel version each provider offers
opts.C: Dependence on provider-specific managed services — the IAM model, the managed database, the queue and the object-storage API — which have no common interface to target
opts.D: Differences in how each provider implements TCP/IP

exp: The compute layer is the part that is already standardised, since OCI-format images and Kubernetes manifests run essentially unchanged on either provider, so the coupling that actually hurts is everything around it: identity and access models, managed database engines and endpoints, queues and storage APIs all differ and must be abstracted or reimplemented per provider. Image formats and TCP/IP are open standards, not points of divergence.

sub: Cloud security and governance: shared responsibility, IAM, Zero Trust, DevSecOps, FinOps and SLAs
q: Under the shared responsibility model, for a virtual machine that a customer runs on an IaaS platform, which of these is the customer's responsibility?

opts.A: Patching the hypervisor on which the virtual machine runs
opts.B: Applying security patches to the guest operating system and the application stack running on that virtual machine
opts.C: Physical access control at the data centre housing the host
opts.D: Replacing failed disks in the underlying storage fabric

exp: The IaaS boundary puts the provider in charge of everything up to and including the virtualization layer and the facility, and the customer in charge of everything from the guest operating system upwards — patching, configuration, identity and data. Hypervisor patching, physical security and hardware replacement all sit below that boundary and remain the provider's obligations.

sub: Cloud security and governance: shared responsibility, IAM, Zero Trust, DevSecOps, FinOps and SLAs
q: A provider's SLA commits to 99.9% availability measured over a 30-day month. What is the maximum downtime that commitment permits in such a month?

opts.A: About 4 minutes 20 seconds
opts.B: About 7 hours 12 minutes
opts.C: About 3 hours 36 minutes
opts.D: About 43 minutes

exp: A 30-day month is 30 x 24 x 60 = 43,200 minutes, and the unavailable allowance is 0.1% of that: 43,200 x 0.001 = 43.2 minutes, or 43 minutes 12 seconds. Each distractor is a neighbouring tier over the same month — 43,200 x 0.0001 = 4.32 minutes is 99.99%, 43,200 x 0.005 = 216 minutes is 99.5%, and 43,200 x 0.01 = 432 minutes, or 7.2 hours, is 99%.

sub: Cloud security and governance: shared responsibility, IAM, Zero Trust, DevSecOps, FinOps and SLAs
q: A FinOps review reports a fleet of 200 always-on virtual machines averaging 4% CPU and 12% memory utilisation over 30 days. Which response is the most direct FinOps action on that finding?

opts.A: Purchase one-year reserved capacity for the fleet at its current instance sizes
opts.B: Rightsize the instances to smaller types and consolidate the workloads, so that both committed spend and idle capacity fall
opts.C: Raise the autoscaling group's maximum size to give the fleet more headroom
opts.D: Move the fleet to a larger instance family so that reported utilisation percentages fall further

exp: FinOps eliminates waste before it optimises rate: 4% average CPU across 200 always-on instances is capacity that is paid for and never used, so rightsizing and consolidation cut the bill at its source — and because an idle server still draws close to its baseline power, the same action is the standard sustainable-cloud lever. Buying a reservation first is the tempting wrong answer, since it only locks the oversized footprint in for a year at a discount.
